title: The fourth jhana
hook: a person wrapped head to foot in clean white cloth (MN 39)

segments.voice: Yesterday: upekkha, and your line, the lotus under water. Did one good moment stay quiet, unposted and untold? Day three hundred ninety-nine, the end of the week.

A clean white cloth, fresh off the line, still cool. Someone sits down, and the cloth is drawn over them from the top of the head to the soles of the feet. Not to hide them. Just to cover them evenly, all the way around. No part warmer than another. No part left out. It's a strange, simple picture, almost nothing happening in it, and that's the point. It's the last of the Buddha's four pictures of deep concentration. Today: the fourth jhana.
screen: `A CLEAN WHITE CLOTH.` → `HEAD TO FOOT, EVENLY.` → `NOTHING LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: MN 39 describes it like this. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the earlier fading of gladness and sorrow, a person enters the fourth jhana: neither painful nor pleasant, with mindfulness made pure by equanimity. They sit pervading the body with a pure, bright mind, the way a person sits wrapped from the head down in white cloth, so that no part of the body isn't covered. Look at the path the four jhanas trace. First, thinking settles. Then the bubbling joy fades. Now even pleasure is let go. Each stage is less, not more. What's left is equanimity and pure mindfulness, like the plain white cloth: no pattern, no color, nothing to grab. Strangely, the suttas treat this not as an ending but as a platform. In MN 36, the Buddha says that on the night of his awakening, with his mind concentrated like this, pure and bright, steady and pliable, he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges followed. And in the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana, DN 16, his last moments pass through the jhanas, and he passes away on emerging from the fourth. So the week ends here: the quail's own ground, the monkey and the pitch, then right concentration and its four pictures: bath powder soaked through, a lake fed by a spring, lotuses under water, and a person wrapped in white. Four pictures, each quieter than the last.
screen: `PLEASURE AND PAIN BOTH LET GO.` · `PURE MINDFULNESS, EQUANIMITY.` · `WRAPPED HEAD TO FOOT IN WHITE.` · `A PLATFORM FOR KNOWING.` · then, large: `WRAPPED IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your attention cover the body evenly, head to foot, the way the cloth covers. No spot more interesting than another. Not chasing a pleasant feeling, not pushing away an unpleasant one. If something itches, it can itch. If something is pleasant, it can be pleasant. Rest in the middle, still, and let it all be covered by plain, clear knowing. The bell holds the time.
Upekkha-sati-parisuddhi, purity of mindfulness through equanimity. Neither pleasure nor pain, only equanimity and pure mindfulness, covering the whole body like clean white cloth.
Your line: wrapped in white. Today, meet one pleasant moment and one unpleasant moment with the same even attention, and notice how that feels. Day three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: In Theravada teaching the fourth jhana is often described as the basis for insight and the higher knowledges; meditators who work with the jhanas usually do so under a teacher; the suttas tell both the Buddha's awakening and his final passing with the fourth jhana.

fork.setup: your mind is still, pure and bright, covered by equanimity like a white cloth. in MN 36, what does the Buddha-to-be do next?
options: stays there as long as possible
directs the clear mind toward knowledge
gets up and goes to find food
fork.reveal: he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges of the night of awakening followed. the stillness was a platform, not the destination.

original.note: Pali upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi: purity of mindfulness through equanimity, the mark of the fourth jhāna.

trapdoor: what you thought: the deepest jhana must be the most blissful.
what it means: even pleasure is let go, leaving equanimity and pure mindfulness, even as a white cloth.
what a scholar hears: the stock phrase upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi, purity of mindfulness through equanimity; in DN 16 the Buddha's final passing follows his emerging from the fourth jhāna.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the white cloth simile)

notes: DN 16: the Buddha passes through the jhanas and attainments, back down, then up to the fourth jhana, and passes away on emerging from it; please confirm the summary.
MN 36: the concentrated mind directed to the three knowledges; please confirm.
